cards.explanation: The answer is weep. Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Ar and Kir were destroyed in a night, so nobody is heading up there for a party. I think this is a town taking its sorrow straight to its temple.

The answer is True. The verse says “on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping.” In its streets they wear sackcloth too. The rooftops and the public squares are both named.

The answer is False. The text says “…the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within.” Even the men trained to hold the line are crying out, friends. When the soldiers are shaking, you know how heavy the moment is.

The answer is that the speaker's heart cries out over Moab, just as the verse says: “My heart cries out over Moab…” This is a burden against Moab, and still the speaker's heart is breaking as the ruin comes into view. I think that tells us how to listen to this prophecy. It's sorrowful, not smug.

The answer is their wealth and belongings. The text says they carry them over the Brook of the Willows. Just before this, the grass is withered and the vegetation is gone. I think a person grabs what they can carry when the ground itself runs dry.
The answer is True. Their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. The wailing reaches Eglaim and is heard in Beer-elim. That's wailing you can hear from place to place, and my oven timer can't do that.

The answer is a lion. The text says “…a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.” The waters of Dimon are already full of blood, and more is coming. It's a heavy verse, friends, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

The answer is the mount of Daughter Zion. The command says to send the tribute lambs from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. They're sent to the ruler of the land, and the verse names that mountain as where they go. Sela in the desert is where they start.

The answer is shelter for the refugees. The plea says “Shelter us at noonday with shade as dark as night. Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees.” They're asking for a place to hide, not a place to fight. I think that's how desperate people ask when they're running.

The answer is David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). The text says a throne will be established in the tent of David, in loving devotion. That comes after the oppressor has gone and destruction has ceased. It's a bright spot in a dark chapter.
The answer is False. The text says the judge is “…seeking justice and hastening righteousness…” He sits on the throne in faithfulness. He hurries toward what is right, not away from it.

The answer is empty. The verse says “But his boasting is empty.” All that pomposity, pride and overflowing arrogance, and the boasting has nothing behind it. It's a big voice with nothing inside, like a fancy cookie box with no cookies.

The answer is that the fields and vines are ruined. The verse gives the reason: “For the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah.” The rulers of the nations have also trampled the choicest vines. I think the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth are a taste of what's been lost.

The answer is that the speaker weeps with Jazer, just like the verse says: “So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah…” The speaker also drenches Heshbon and Elealeh with tears. I think that's someone who isn't standing at a distance, but crying right alongside Jazer.

The answer is True. The verse says “Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres.” The lament reaches the speaker's inmost being. I think it sounds like a harp playing a sad song.

The answer is False. The verse says that when Moab appears on the high place, wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, “…it will do him no good.” Wearing himself out doesn't change that, friends. The verse says it plainly.

The answer is an object of contempt. The LORD says “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people.” A hired worker counts the years carefully, and this is the count. The splendor won't stay splendid.
The answer is False. The LORD says “And those who are left will be few and feeble.” That's the opposite of many and strong. It's a sober ending to a heavy passage.
